questions.question: What is the core correctness invariant of an MoE layer?
options: Every token must execute every expert
Every admitted token must complete the intended available expert paths within capacity and return one correctly weighted result
Every expert must receive exactly the same token text
Only the router must fit in accelerator memory
questions.explanation: Sparse execution is correct only when admitted assignments reach available experts, stay within the defined capacity behavior, and recombine into the right token output.

questions.question: A batch has 32,768 tokens, top-2 routing, 32 experts, and a capacity factor of 1.25. What is the planned capacity per expert?
options: 1,024 assignments
2,048 assignments
2,560 assignments
65,536 assignments
questions.explanation: There are 65,536 assignments, or 2,048 per expert at perfect balance. Multiplying by 1.25 gives 2,560.

questions.question: Why does activating 2 of 64 experts not reduce expert-weight storage by 96.875%?
options: The router duplicates every token 64 times
Inactive experts still require their weights to be resident somewhere the serving topology can reach
Expert weights are stored inside the tokenizer
Sparse models cannot use reduced precision
questions.explanation: Sparse activation reduces per-token expert compute, but all unique expert parameters still exist and must be stored, loaded, versioned, and recovered.

questions.question: The expert loads are balanced, but all-to-all p99 is high on one network cut. Which response most directly addresses the failed stage?
options: Increase the capacity factor
Make every router logit larger
Use topology-aware placement and locality-aware dispatch
Remove all routing telemetry
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is token movement, so placement and routing locality target the congested path. More expert slots do not add network bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the main risk of using a strong load-balancing loss?
options: It can force traffic toward uniformity and erase useful expert specialization
It removes all expert parameters from the checkpoint
It makes top-K greater than the expert count
It disables the model's attention layers
questions.explanation: Balancing pressure prevents collapse, but excessive pressure can override semantic routing patterns that improve task quality.

questions.question: An expert-owning device fails while the router still selects its experts. What is required for bounded availability?
options: A higher router entropy metric only
A version-compatible replica, compatible reroute, or evaluated fallback path
A larger tokenizer vocabulary
A lower batch identifier
questions.explanation: Spare capacity cannot execute missing weights. The serving contract needs another compatible path and must test its latency and quality.

questions.question: Which telemetry best separates routing imbalance from network saturation?
options: Only end-to-end request count
Expert assignment histograms plus source-destination dispatch bytes and queue time
Only checkpoint file size
Only the average training loss
questions.explanation: Assignments reveal router concentration, while pairwise bytes and queue time reveal whether movement across the expert topology is the bottleneck.

questions.question: When is a tuned dense model often preferable to MoE?
options: When small batches and strict tail latency make distributed routing overhead dominate the quality gain
Whenever more than one accelerator exists
Whenever a model uses attention
Only when the model has no feed-forward layers
questions.explanation: MoE must beat a dense baseline on the actual quality-cost frontier. Small batches, strict tails, weak interconnects, or modest gains can favor dense execution.
